soft_issues: Consensus signal and controversy role are marked as strong agreement and neutral, respectively, but the extract mentions potential contributions from sea lice, which could introduce some controversy.

claim_checks.claim: Wild 1SW River Imsa salmon: mean LT fell 63→54 cm (1976–2010 regressions, r²≈0.51), ~40% mass decline (2.0→1.2 kg); hatchery releases show parallel trends (r²≈0.36 for LT).
claim_checks.extract_quote: Annual mean total length (LT) of wild one-sea-winter (1SW) Atlantic salmon Salmo salar of the Norwegian River Imsa decreased from 63 to 54cm with a corresponding decrease in condition factor (K) for cohorts migrating to sea from 1976 to 2010.

claim_checks.claim: 1SW LT negatively correlated with Norwegian Sea summer/winter SST (e.g. wild summer slope −28.6 mm °C⁻¹, p<0.05) but temperature explains only modest variance (r²≈0.13–0.32).
claim_checks.extract_quote: The LT of 1SW fish decreased with increasing ocean temperature. The slope of the regression was steeper for hatchery than wild S. salar [Table II(a); summer temperature: F1,57 =8⋅8, P<0⋅01].

claim_checks.claim: 36,201 wild smolts (1976–2010), 2.9% adult return; 182,740 hatchery smolts (1981–2010), 1.5% return—hatchery mirrors wild life-history shifts (LT, K, G, %1SW: r² 0.37–0.71).
claim_checks.extract_quote: From 1976 to 2010, 36201 wild smolts migrated from the river to the sea, and tagging studies suggest that they fed in the north Norwegian Sea... Of these, 2⋅9% returned to the trap in the river as adults.

claim_checks.claim: Post-smolt growth (G) positively linked to adult LT and wild marine survival (S); proportion maturing as 1SW peaks mid-series (Weibull fits) and tracks condition factor in hatchery fish.
claim_checks.extract_quote: In wild S. salar, there was a positive association between post-smolt growth and the sea survival back to the River Imsa for spawning.

claim_checks.claim: Authors attribute trends to North Atlantic food-web restructuring (pelagic collapse/rebuild, zooplankton decline) plus ~1°C SST rise—not direct lice or aquaculture effects.
claim_checks.extract_quote: An additional possible reason for the decrease in growth and K with time could be the recent increase in abundance of sea lice Lepeophtheirus salmonis, which can affect post-smolt growth and survival negatively.
claim_checks.note: The extract mentions sea lice as a potential factor, which contradicts the summary's claim that lice are not considered.

evidence_direction_note: The summary emphasizes environmental changes as the primary driver, but the extract also mentions potential contributions from sea lice, which is not highlighted in the summary.
